title: Senior Backend Engineer Interview - Ravi Shankar
segments: Hi Ravi, thanks for joining. I'm Alex, I run engineering here, and Marcus is one of our senior backend engineers. We'll spend about forty minutes, with time at the end for your questions.
Thanks for having me. I'm excited to learn more about the team.
To start, could you tell us about a recent project you're proud of?

Sure. At my current company I led the redesign of our notification pipeline. It was a single Python service that sent roughly two million messages a day and was falling over whenever a provider had an outage.
I split it into a producer that writes to Kafka and a set of independent workers per channel, each with its own retry policy and a dead letter queue.
What drove the decision to use Kafka rather than something simpler like SQS?

Honestly it was partly that we already ran Kafka for analytics. But the real reason was replay. When a provider bug dropped messages for an hour, we could rewind the consumer offset and resend, which wasn't possible with SQS.
That's a fair reason. Did you run into ordering problems?
Yes. We needed per-user ordering, so we keyed by user ID. The downside was a few very active accounts created hot partitions, and we had to add a secondary key for bulk senders.
Good. Let's shift to something more design oriented. Imagine we need a rate limiter for our public API. How would you approach it?
I'd start by clarifying requirements. Is it per API key, per IP, per endpoint? And do we need it to be exact or is approximate fine?
Per API key, and approximate is fine, but it needs to work across multiple API servers.

Then I'd use a token bucket stored in Redis. Each request runs a small Lua script that refills the bucket based on elapsed time and takes a token atomically, so there are no race conditions between servers.
I'd fail open with a local in-memory limiter as a fallback, with a lower limit per server. Taking the API down because the rate limiter is down seems like the worse failure.
I agree with that. How would you tell clients they've been limited?
A 429 status with a Retry-After header, plus the standard rate limit headers on every response so well behaved clients can slow down before they hit the wall.
Nice. Let's talk about something that went wrong. Tell us about a production incident you were part of.
A few months ago we shipped a migration that added an index on a table with about four hundred million rows. We ran it during business hours and it locked writes for eleven minutes.
I was on call. We couldn't cancel it safely, so we waited it out while I handled communication with support and the customers affected.

Three things. We moved to concurrent index creation, we required a migration review for any table over a million rows, and we added a staging environment with production sized data so we'd see the timing before it mattered.
I like that the fix was process as well as tooling. Let me ask a more hands on question. How would you debug an endpoint that's suddenly slow?

First I'd check whether it's slow for everyone or a subset, using traces to see which span grew. Then I'd look at the database, usually slow queries or lock contention, before suspecting the application code.
And if the traces show the time is in a downstream service?
Then I'd look at that service's own metrics, check timeouts and retries, because retries can multiply load during a slowdown. Sometimes the fix is a circuit breaker, not a faster query.
That's the answer I was hoping for. Let's do some coding talk. What's your approach to testing a service that talks to external APIs?

A mix. Unit tests with the client mocked at the boundary, contract tests against recorded responses, and a small number of end to end tests against a sandbox. I try to keep the end to end set tiny because they're flaky.
How do you keep recorded responses from going stale?
A scheduled job re-records them weekly and opens a pull request if anything differs. That way API changes show up as a diff instead of a production surprise.
That's clever. Now, how do you like to work with product and design?
I like being involved early. Engineers often spot cheaper ways to get the same outcome, and I'd rather suggest a simpler version in week one than argue about scope in week six.
Good. Anything you'd like to ask us?
Yes. What does on call look like here, and how often would I be on the rotation?
It's one week in six, and we have a runbook for every alert. We also have a rule that any alert that pages someone at night gets a ticket to fix the root cause.
That's healthier than my current place. What's the biggest technical challenge the team faces this year?
Scaling our ingestion pipeline. Carrier updates are growing about eighty percent year over year, and the current design won't make it past next summer without changes.
That's right in the area I've been working in. I'd enjoy that.
Great. What's your timeline? Are you talking to other companies?
I have two other final rounds next week. I'd love to decide within about ten days.
Understood. We'll debrief this afternoon and I'll get back to you by Monday with next steps.
Perfect. Thanks to you both, I really enjoyed the conversation.
Take care, and we'll be in touch.
overview: Technical interview for a senior backend engineer role. Ravi described redesigning a two-million-messages-a-day notification pipeline around Kafka, with per-channel workers and dead letter queues, and discussed ordering and hot partition tradeoffs. He designed a Redis token bucket rate limiter that fails open to a local limiter, walked through a production incident where an index migration locked a 400M-row table for eleven minutes and the process changes that followed, and outlined a debugging approach built on traces and circuit breakers. The interviewers were impressed with his testing strategy. Ravi asked about on-call load and the team's biggest challenge, scaling ingestion. Alex will follow up by Monday.
